title: Random walks on networks
objectives: Find the stationary distribution of a random walk on a weighted network
Compute mean return times as the reciprocal of the share
Use the degree count for the knight's return time

screens.title: Where does the router spend its time?
screens.prose: Four venues are linked as shown. An order router starts at D and hops along a random link each step. Slide through one seeded run and watch each venue fill with its share of visits.

frames.caption: After 10 steps the walker is at B.
After 50 steps the walker is at C.
After 200 steps the walker is at C.
After 1,000 steps the walker is at B.
After 10,000 steps the walker is at A.

screens.question: After 10,000 steps, which venue has the largest share of visits?

options.text: A, the venue with the most links

options.why: You expected an even split. At 10,000 steps A holds about 0.37 and D only 0.12.
A start is forgotten in the long run. D has the smallest share, about 0.12.

options.text: B and C, because they are linked to each other
options.why: B and C share a link, but A has three. B and C each sit near 0.25.

hints.text: Slide to the longest run and read the four shares.
Compare the shares with how many links each venue has.
A has 3 links, B and C have 2, and D has 1.

feedback.correct: A has the most links and the largest share.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide to 10,000 steps and read the four shares.

explain.text: At 10,000 steps the shares are about 0.37, 0.25, 0.26 and 0.12 for A, B, C and D. The venue with more links is visited more. D has one link and is visited least.

screens.title: Count the links
screens.prose: A link joins two venues, so it counts for both of them. The number of links at a venue is its **degree**. The shares were near 0.37, 0.25, 0.25 and 0.12.
screens.question: Count each venue's degree, and the total over all four.

hints.text: Count the lines touching each venue.
B touches A and C. The total adds the four degrees.
Degrees 3, 2, 2 and 1 add to 8.

feedback.correct: The degrees are 3, 2, 2 and 1, and they add to 8.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the lines touching each venue, and add the four counts.

byKey.r4c1: The total adds the four degrees, 3 + 2 + 2 + 1. It is not the number of links, which is 4.

explain.text: The degrees add to 8, twice the 4 links, because every link has two ends. The shares $\tfrac38, \tfrac28, \tfrac28, \tfrac18$ match 0.37, 0.25, 0.25 and 0.12.

screens.title: Test the guess
screens.prose: The shares look like degree over total degree: $\pi_i = \tfrac{\deg(i)}{8}$. We test that guess. A fifth venue E joins, linked to A only.
screens.question: What share of the time is the walker at D now?

hints.text: D still has 1 link. What is the new total of degrees?
E adds one link, which adds 2 to the total.
The total is 10, so D gets $\tfrac{1}{10}$.

feedback.correct: D has degree 1 of a total of 10, so $\tfrac{1}{10}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the new degree of each venue, add them, and take D's share.

byKey.unchanged: You kept the old total 8. The new link adds 1 to the degree of A and 1 to E, so the total is 10.
byKey.nodes: You gave every venue an equal share. Shares follow degree, not headcount.
byKey.links: You used 1 over the 4 old links. Divide by the total degree 10.

explain.text: The degrees are $4, 2, 2, 1, 1$ for A, B, C, D, E, adding to 10. So D gets $\tfrac{1}{10}$, down from $\tfrac18$. Adding a link anywhere takes time from every other venue.

screens.title: Why degree over total
screens.prose: Why does degree over total work? We check detailed balance for the weights $\deg(i)$. Write $|E|$ for the number of links.
screens.question: Put the lines of the argument in order.

lines.text: From $i$ the walker picks one of its $\deg(i)$ links evenly, so $P_{ij} = \tfrac{1}{\deg(i)}$ for each neighbour $j$
For linked $i, j$: $\deg(i)P_{ij} = 1$ and $\deg(j)P_{ji} = 1$, since each is a degree times its own $\tfrac{1}{\deg}$
So $\deg(i)P_{ij} = \deg(j)P_{ji}$: detailed balance holds, and for unlinked pairs both sides are 0
Each link has two ends, so $\sum_i \deg(i) = 2|E|$
Divide by that total: $\pi_i = \dfrac{\deg(i)}{2|E|}$ adds to 1 and is stationary by detailed balance

hints.text: Start with the walker's rule for choosing a link.
Check balance first, then normalise.
Rule, equal products, balance, total degree, shares.

feedback.correct: $\pi_i = \deg(i)/2|E|$ satisfies detailed balance, so it is stationary.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Begin with the choice of link, then check balance, then divide by the total.

byKey.o2: The products need the formula for $P_{ij}$ first.
byKey.o3: Balance follows from the two products, so they come first.
byKey.o4: The total comes after balance holds for the weights.

explain.text: The walker chooses links evenly, so $\deg(i)P_{ij} = 1$ in both directions. Balance holds for the weights $\deg(i)$. Dividing by their total $2|E|$ gives shares that add to 1.

screens.title: Return times
screens.prose: Back to the four venues, with $\pi_D = \tfrac18$. Over 800 steps the router is at D about 100 times. Visits to D are spread out in time.
screens.question: On average, how many steps pass between one visit to D and the next?

hints.text: About 100 visits in 800 steps. How far apart are they?
800 divided by 100.
The mean gap is $1/\pi_D = 8$.

feedback.correct: The mean return time to D is $1/\pi_D = 8$ steps.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. If D holds a share $\pi$ of the steps, visits come every $1/\pi$ steps.

byKey.share: That is the share of steps at D. The gap between visits is its reciprocal.
byKey.nodes: You used the number of venues. The gap depends on D's share, $\tfrac18$.
byKey.between: You counted the steps strictly between visits. The return time counts the step that arrives, so it is 8.
byKey.degree-ratio: You used A's degree. D has degree 1, so $\pi_D = \tfrac18$ and the gap is 8.

explain.text: D holds $\tfrac18$ of all steps, so visits come once per 8 steps on average. In general the mean return time to a state is $1/\pi_i$. For A it is $\tfrac83$, so the router passes A often.

screens.title: Links with strengths
screens.prose: Links now have strengths. The walker leaves a venue along a link with chance proportional to its strength. Then $\pi_i$ is proportional to the total strength at $i$, in place of $\deg(i)$.

state.caption: Link strengths are on the edges.

screens.question: What is the mean number of steps between visits to B?

hints.text: Add the strengths of the links touching B. Then add the strengths at all three venues.
B has 1 + 2 = 3. A has 1 + 3 = 4, and C has 2 + 3 = 5.
The total is 12, so $\pi_B = \tfrac{3}{12}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find B's total strength and the all-venue total, then invert the share.

byKey.nodes: You used the number of venues. The return time is $1/\pi_B$.
byKey.half-total: You divided by the sum of link strengths, 6. Each link counts at both ends, so the total is 12.
byKey.share: That is $\pi_B$. The return time is its reciprocal.

explain.text: B's strength is $1 + 2 = 3$ and the total is $2 \times (1 + 2 + 3) = 12$. So $\pi_B = \tfrac14$ and the router returns to B every 4 steps. The sum of strengths over venues is twice the sum over links.

screens.title: The knight's degrees
screens.prose: A knight on a chessboard moves to a random legal square each step. The board shows the number of moves from each square. A corner has 2.

state.caption: Each square shows the number of squares a knight can reach from it.

screens.question: Add up the degrees of all 64 squares by type.

hints.text: Multiply the number of moves by the number of squares of that type.
For degree 3: 8 squares, each with 3 moves.
The five products are 8, 24, 80, 96 and 128. Add them.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each row, multiply moves by squares, then add the five products.

byKey.r0c2: Four corner squares with 2 moves each add 8.
byKey.r1c2: Eight squares with 3 moves each add 24.
byKey.r2c2: Twenty squares with 4 moves each add 80.
byKey.r3c2: Sixteen squares with 6 moves each add 96.
byKey.r4c2: Sixteen squares with 8 moves each add 128.

explain.text: The products are $8, 24, 80, 96$ and $128$, and they add to 336. That is $2|E|$ for the knight's graph, so there are 168 legal moves from square to square.

screens.title: A corner's return time
screens.prose: The knight starts in a corner. On this graph $\pi_i = \deg(i)/336$. A famous interview question asks how long it takes the knight to return to its starting square, on average.

state.caption: Each square shows the number of squares a knight can reach from it.

screens.question: What is the mean return time to a corner?

hints.text: A corner has degree 2. What is its share of the 336?
$\pi_{\text{corner}} = \tfrac{2}{336}$.
The mean return time is $1/\pi = 336/2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the corner's share $\tfrac{2}{336}$ and invert it.

byKey.squares: You used the number of squares. Squares are not equally likely, so the return time uses the corner's own share.
byKey.total: You forgot to divide by the corner's degree 2.
byKey.interior: You used a degree-8 square: 336/8. The corner has degree 2.
byKey.four: You divided by 4, the number of corners. Use the degree of one corner, 2.

explain.text: A corner has share $\tfrac{2}{336}$, so the knight returns every $\tfrac{336}{2} = 168$ moves on average. A central square with degree 8 is revisited every 42 moves. The board does not need solving: degrees are enough.

screens.title: A square has period 2
screens.prose: Four venues form a square. Every degree is 2, so $\pi = (\tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac14)$ is stationary. The walker starts at A and takes exactly 1,001 steps.
screens.question: What is the chance the walker is at A at step 1,001?

hints.text: Every step moves between the pair {A, C} and the pair {B, D}.
After an odd number of steps the walker is at B or D.
1,001 is odd, so it cannot be at A.

feedback.correct: After an odd number of steps the walker is at B or D, never at A.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Track which pair the walker is in after each step.

byKey.pi: That is the long-run share of time at A, which is right. But the chance at one fixed step never settles at it.
byKey.half: Half is the chance of each of B and D. A is impossible at odd steps.
byKey.two: You divided $\tfrac14$ by 2. At step 1,001 the walker cannot be at A.

explain.text: Each step swaps between {A, C} and {B, D}, so $P^k$ alternates and never converges. The time share at A is still $\tfrac14$, as in lesson 6. A walk on a network with no odd cycles is periodic like this.

screens.title: Not equal time
screens.prose: A colleague models orders hopping between a hub H and three leaf venues. Each leaf links only to H. She says: a random walk spends the same time at every venue, so the hub gets $\tfrac14$.

state.caption: A hub H with three leaves.

screens.question: What share of the time is the walker at the hub?

options.why: You gave every venue the same share. The hub has three links and each leaf has one.
You divided the hub's degree 3 by the number of venues, 4. Degrees add to 6, since each link has two ends.
That is a leaf's share, $\tfrac16$. The hub has degree 3 of the total 6.

hints.text: Find the degree of the hub and of each leaf.
The hub has degree 3 and each leaf has degree 1.
The degrees add to $3 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6$.

feedback.correct: Degree 3 out of a total of 6 gives $\tfrac12$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the hub's degree by the total degree, not by the number of venues.

byKey.equal: You gave every venue the same share. The hub has three links and each leaf has one.
byKey.nodes: You divided by the number of venues, 4. The shares would then add to more than 1: the total to divide by is $2|E| = 6$.
byKey.leaf: That is a leaf's share, not the hub's.

explain.text: Every second step is at the hub: leaves can only go to H, and H goes to a leaf. So the share at H is $\tfrac12$, matching $\tfrac{3}{6}$. Equal shares hold only when every degree is equal.

screens.title: A dealer network
screens.prose: Five dealers pass quotes only along the links shown. Each quote moves to a random linked dealer, one hop at a time. Over a long day the flow through each dealer follows its degree.

state.caption: Quotes pass along links between dealers.

screens.question: What share of all quote visits goes through dealer D1?

hints.text: Count the links at D1, then every dealer's links.
D1 has 4. The others have 2, 3, 2 and 1.
The degrees add to 12, so D1 gets $\tfrac{4}{12}$.

feedback.correct: D1 has degree 4 of a total of 12, a third of all visits.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide D1's degree by the total degree of all five dealers.

byKey.equal: You gave each dealer an equal share. D1 has the most links.
byKey.links: You divided D1's 4 links by the 6 links. Divide by the total degree, 12.

explain.text: The degrees are 4, 2, 3, 2 and 1, adding to 12, so D1 sees $\tfrac13$ of all quote flow. One dealer carries a third of the flow, a single point of failure. That is an argument for a central counterparty.

ideas: A random walk on an undirected network is reversible with $\pi_i = \dfrac{\deg(i)}{2|E|}$. With link strengths, replace the degree by the total strength at $i$.
The mean return time to a state is $1/\pi_i$. For the knight, a corner has degree 2 of a total 336, so it returns every 168 moves.
Shares follow degree, not headcount. A bipartite network has a stationary $\pi$ but its $P^k$ does not converge. A network in two pieces has more than one $\pi$.

formula.name: Walk on a network
formula.note: Weighted: $\pi_i$ is the strength at $i$ over the total strength.

summary.trap: Dividing a degree by the number of venues. The degrees add to $2|E|$, so that is the divisor.

quiz.prose: A random walk on a connected network has the same long-run share at every venue.
quiz.question: When does this happen?

options.text: When every venue has the same degree
Always, since the walker moves at random
options.why: Random moves do not mean equal shares. The share follows the degree.

options.text: Only when the network is bipartite
options.why: A star is bipartite and has very unequal shares. Equal degrees are what matter.

options.text: Only when there are many venues
options.why: Size does not matter. A square with 4 venues has equal shares, a star with 100 does not.

feedback.correct: Shares are proportional to degrees, so they are equal exactly when the degrees are.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall that the share is the degree over $2|E|$.

explain.text: The share of venue $i$ is $\deg(i)/2|E|$. Shares are equal exactly when all degrees are equal, as on a square.
